key_terms.meaning: σ/y = M/I = E/R for bending about a principal axis; σ in N/mm², M in N·mm, I in mm⁴.
Z = I/y<sub>max</sub>; a section not symmetric about its neutral axis has Z<sub>top</sub> and Z<sub>bot</sub>.
1/R′ = ν/R, the opposite-sense curl of a free cross-section; restrained, it becomes a transverse stress νσ.
x horizontal, y up, z along the beam; M<sub>x</sub> > 0 puts positive y in tension, M<sub>y</sub> > 0 puts positive x in tension.
I<sub>xy</sub> = ∫x y dA about centroidal axes; zero if the section has an axis of symmetry.
σ = [(M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xx</sub> − M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)x + (M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)y]/D, D = I<sub>xx</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − I<sub>xy</sub>².
tan α = (M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub> − M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xx</sub>)/(M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>), from the x axis.
tan 2θ = −2I<sub>xy</sub>/(I<sub>xx</sub> − I<sub>yy</sub>); I<sub>u</sub>, I<sub>v</sub> = (I<sub>xx</sub> + I<sub>yy</sub>)/2 ± √[((I<sub>xx</sub> − I<sub>yy</sub>)/2)² + I<sub>xy</sub>²].
σ = M<sub>NA</sub> n/I<sub>NA</sub>, with n the distance from the neutral axis.

u″ = (M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub> − M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xx</sub>)/(E D), v″ = (M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xy</sub> − M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>yy</sub>)/(E D); the beam deflects perpendicular to the neutral axis.
I<sub>xx,0</sub> = t s³ sin²θ/12, I<sub>yy,0</sub> = t s³ cos²θ/12, I<sub>xy,0</sub> = t s³ sin θ cos θ/12; t³ terms dropped.
A stringer plus effective skin lumped as an area carrying direct stress.
1/R<sub>T</sub> = α(T<sub>top</sub> − T<sub>bot</sub>)/h, with no stress in a free beam.
σ<sub>i</sub> = −E α T<sub>i</sub> + N<sub>T</sub>/A + general formula with M<sub>xT</sub>, M<sub>yT</sub>.

takeaways: About a principal axis, σ = M y/I and 1/R = M/(E I); the neutral axis passes through the centroid.
Poisson's ratio curls a free cross-section to R′ = R/ν; held flat, the skin carries a transverse stress νσ.
With I<sub>xy</sub> ≠ 0 the stress is σ = k₁ x + k₂ y and the neutral axis tilts towards the flexible direction.
The k, neutral axis and principal axis methods are one formula; each gives the same stress at a point.
The beam deflects perpendicular to its neutral axis, so a Z-section loaded downwards moves sideways too.
Thin walls are mid-lines with t³ terms dropped; offset walls need their parallel-axis terms, and the signs of x<sub>c</sub> and y<sub>c</sub> set the sign of I<sub>xy</sub>.
Unequal booms on a rectangle give I<sub>xy</sub> ≠ 0; lift and drag give negative M<sub>x</sub> and M<sub>y</sub> at a wing station in this convention.
A linear temperature field bends a free beam without stress; restraint or a non-linear field produces stress.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the general unsymmetrical bending formula, the neutral axis and the stress at chosen points of an angle, channel or Z-section, often by a named method (neutral axis, k or principal axis), and then the deflection of the same beam. Show the section-property table and state the sign convention.

glossary.def: Curl of a cross-section opposite to the bending, caused by Poisson's ratio; radius R/ν.
The internal moment at a section, in N·mm or N·m, equal to the moment of all loads on one side.
A concentrated area standing for a stringer and its effective skin; it carries direct stress only.
The point about which the first moment of area is zero; the neutral axis passes through it in pure bending.
α, the free strain per kelvin; about 23 × 10⁻⁶ per K for aluminium.
Normal stress along the beam, in N/mm²; positive in tension.
E I, the resistance of a beam to curvature.
The general unsymmetrical formula written with section constants I<sub>yy</sub>/D, I<sub>xx</sub>/D and I<sub>xy</sub>/D.
The centre line of a thin wall, along which lengths and positions are measured.
The line of zero direct stress through the centroid.
Finding the neutral axis first and taking the stress as M<sub>NA</sub> n/I<sub>NA</sub>.
ν, the ratio of lateral contraction to axial extension; about 0.33 for aluminium alloys.
The pair of centroidal axes about which I<sub>uv</sub> = 0 and the second moments are largest and smallest.
Resolving the moment onto the principal axes and adding two symmetrical-bending stresses.
I<sub>xy</sub> = ∫x y dA, in mm⁴; positive, negative or zero.
I = ∫y² dA about an axis, in mm⁴.
Z = I/y<sub>max</sub>, in mm³; σ<sub>max</sub> = M/Z.
A stress field with zero net force and zero net moments, such as the thermal stress of a free beam with a non-linear temperature.
Uneven direct stress across a wide skin, higher near the webs than between them.
A load not along a principal axis, giving moments about both axes.
A longitudinal stiffener riveted or bonded to the skin.
A section whose walls are thin compared with their length, so stress is uniform across the thickness.
Bending in which the moment is not about a principal axis, so the neutral axis is not along the moment axis.
A stringer shape with two flanges pointing opposite ways; it has no axis of symmetry and a large I<sub>xy</sub>.

bank.q: Derive the bending formula σ/y = M/I = E/R for symmetrical bending, stating every assumption, and define the section modulus.
outline: σ = E y/R by Hooke's law
Zero axial force puts the neutral axis at the centroid
Moment equilibrium gives M = E I/R
Z = I/y<sub>max</sub> and two moduli for unsymmetric depth
answer: Assumptions: plane sections remain plane and normal to the bent axis; deflections are small; the material is linear elastic with the same E in tension and compression; the moment acts about a principal axis; no axial force acts.

answer.text: Geometry. Two sections a distance dz apart rotate through dφ about the neutral axis, whose radius is R. A fibre at distance y from the neutral axis has length (R + y) dφ after bending, against R dφ before, so its strain is:
answer.pre: ε = [(R + y) dφ − R dφ]/(R dφ) = y/R

answer: Stress. Hooke's law gives σ = E ε = E y/R: the stress varies linearly with y and is zero on the neutral axis.

answer.text: Force equilibrium. With no axial force:
answer.pre: ∫σ dA = (E/R) ∫y dA = 0  →  ∫y dA = 0

answer: The first moment of area is zero only about the centroid, so the neutral axis passes through the centroid of the section.

answer.text: Moment equilibrium. The stresses must add up to the applied moment:
answer.pre: M = ∫σ y dA = (E/R) ∫y² dA = E I/R

answer.text: Combine the two results (E/R = σ/y and E/R = M/I):
answer.pre: σ/y = M/I = E/R,   σ = M y/I,   1/R = M/(E I)

answer: Each term: σ is the direct stress at distance y from the neutral axis (N/mm²), M the bending moment (N·mm), I the second moment of area about the neutral axis (mm⁴), E Young's modulus (N/mm²) and R the radius of curvature (mm).

Section modulus. The largest stress is at the farthest fibre: σ<sub>max</sub> = M y<sub>max</sub>/I = M/Z with Z = I/y<sub>max</sub>. A section that is not symmetric about its neutral axis has two moduli, Z<sub>top</sub> and Z<sub>bot</sub>, and the smaller one governs yield.

Limits in an aircraft structure: the moment must act about a principal axis (otherwise use the unsymmetrical formula); shear lag in wide skins, local buckling of thin compressed walls and plasticity near ultimate load all make the real peak stress differ from M y/I.

Sign convention: with y measured upwards and M positive when it puts positive y in tension, σ = M y/I gives tension above and compression below the neutral axis for M > 0, and the opposite for M < 0; a wing with upward lift has negative M at the root.

Check with numbers: for I = 8.5 × 10⁶ mm⁴, y<sub>max</sub> = 100 mm and M = 20 kN·m, σ<sub>max</sub> = 2 × 10⁷ × 100/8.5 × 10⁶ = 235.3 N/mm², and for E = 70,000 N/mm² the radius is R = E I/M = 29,750 mm, with y<sub>max</sub>/R = 3.36 × 10⁻³ = σ/E, as the formula requires.

bank.q: What is anticlastic bending? Derive the relation between the anticlastic and the longitudinal curvature, and explain what happens when the curl is restrained.
answer: Definition. Anticlastic bending is the curvature of the cross-section, in its own plane, in the opposite sense to the longitudinal curvature of the beam.

Origin. A bent beam has longitudinal strain ε = y/R. By Poisson's ratio ν, every fibre also strains sideways by −ν ε = −ν y/R. The tension side (y > 0 for a positive moment) contracts sideways and the compression side expands.

answer.text: Curvature of the section. The sideways strain varies linearly with y, exactly as the longitudinal strain does, so the section bends sideways with a curvature equal to the gradient of the sideways strain:
answer.pre: d(sideways strain)/dy = −ν/R   →   1/R′ = ν/R,   R′ = R/ν

answer: The minus sign is the opposite sense: a beam bending into a valley along its length bends into a hill across its width. The surface is a saddle.

Size. For aluminium (ν = 0.33) R′ ≈ 3R. In the worked example R = 29.75 m gives R′ = 29.75/0.33 = 90.2 m. On a 2 mm strip bent to R = 20 m with ν = 0.30, R′ = 66.7 m and the face strain is ±1.5 × 10⁻⁵ sideways.
When the curl is free. Only on a narrow strip or near a free edge, cut-out or hole.

answer.text: When it is restrained. In a wide plate or a stiffened box the skin, stringers and ribs keep the section flat. The sideways strain must then be zero:
answer.pre: ε<sub>t</sub> = (σ<sub>t</sub> − ν σ)/E = 0   →   σ<sub>t</sub> = ν σ

answer: The transverse stress has the same sign as the bending stress: the tension skin also carries transverse tension, and the compression skin transverse compression. The skin works biaxially, which affects fatigue at fasteners and the buckling of compression panels. A wide plate held flat is also stiffer than a beam by the factor 1/(1 − ν²).

Why it matters in an exam answer: the relation 1/R′ = ν/R is used to explain why a bent ruler or a thin aircraft panel looks saddle-shaped, why strain gauges on a bent plate read a sideways strain, and why the plate formula uses D = E t³/[12(1 − ν²)] instead of E I: a wide plate cannot curl, so it is stiffer than a narrow beam of the same depth.
Check: σ = M y/I is unchanged in both cases; only the shape of the section and the transverse stress differ.

bank.q: Explain why the neutral axis of a section with I<sub>xy</sub> ≠ 0 does not lie along the axis of the applied moment. Derive tan α for the general case.
outline: σ = k₁x + k₂y and the two moment conditions
Physical reason and the Z-section example
answer: In symmetrical bending under M<sub>x</sub> alone, the stress is M<sub>x</sub> y/I<sub>xx</sub> and the neutral axis is the x axis, the axis the moment acts about. This holds only when x is a principal axis, I<sub>xy</sub> = 0.

answer.text: General case. Plane sections give a stress linear in x and y, σ = k₁ x + k₂ y (zero at the centroid since there is no axial force). The moment conditions are:
answer.pre:
M<sub>x</sub> = ∫σ y dA = k₁ I<sub>xy</sub> + k₂ I<sub>xx</sub>
M<sub>y</sub> = ∫σ x dA = k₁ I<sub>yy</sub> + k₂ I<sub>xy</sub>

answer.text: Solving the two equations:
answer.pre: k₁ = (M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xx</sub> − M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D,   k₂ = (M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D,   D = I<sub>xx</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − I<sub>xy</sub>²

answer.text: Neutral axis. Setting σ = 0 gives a straight line through the centroid:
answer.pre: k₁ x + k₂ y = 0   →   tan α = y/x = −k₁/k₂ = (M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub> − M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xx</sub>)/(M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)

answer: With M<sub>y</sub> = 0, tan α = I<sub>xy</sub>/I<sub>yy</sub>. The neutral axis therefore lies along the moment axis (α = 0) only when I<sub>xy</sub> = 0. Any product second moment tilts it.

Physical picture. The section is coupled: a moment about x alone must produce a stress varying with x, because otherwise the stresses would give a moment about y. The stress field rotates towards the direction in which the section is most flexible.

Example. For the Z-section with I<sub>xx</sub> = 666,667 mm⁴, I<sub>yy</sub> = 166,667 mm⁴ and I<sub>xy</sub> = 250,000 mm⁴ under M<sub>x</sub> alone, tan α = 250,000/166,667 = 1.5 and α = 56.3°. The neutral axis is far from the x axis.

Consequence for stress. The largest stress is at the point farthest from the tilted neutral axis. For the Z-section that is the web–flange corner (171.4 MPa for M<sub>x</sub> = 1 kN·m), not the flange tip (−85.7 MPa), and the simple formula would have given 75.0 MPa at both.

Special case of a moment about a principal axis: if the moment acts about a principal axis (u or v), the stress is simply M y/I about that axis and the neutral axis lies along it, even when I<sub>xy</sub> ≠ 0 about the original x and y axes.
Consequence for deflection. The beam deflects at right angles to the neutral axis, so it does not move in the plane of the load.

bank.q: State the approximations used for thin-walled sections and discuss the applicability of simple bending theory to them.
answer: Thin wall: thickness t small compared with length s (t/s below about 0.1).
Approximation 1: the direct stress is uniform across t, so each wall is drawn as its mid-line.
Approximation 2: lengths are measured along the mid-line and corner overlaps are ignored.

answer.text: Approximation 3: terms in t² and t³ are dropped. A straight wall at angle θ then has, about its own centroid:
answer.pre: I<sub>xx,0</sub> = t s³ sin²θ/12,  I<sub>yy,0</sub> = t s³ cos²θ/12,  I<sub>xy,0</sub> = t s³ sin θ cos θ/12

answer: Approximation 4: stringers become booms, concentrated areas with no second moment of their own.

answer.text: Section properties then follow from sums over walls and booms, with each wall's centroid (x<sub>c</sub>, y<sub>c</sub>) measured from the section centroid:
answer.pre: I<sub>xx</sub> = Σ(I<sub>xx,0</sub> + a y<sub>c</sub>²),  I<sub>yy</sub> = Σ(I<sub>yy,0</sub> + a x<sub>c</sub>²),  I<sub>xy</sub> = Σ(I<sub>xy,0</sub> + a x<sub>c</sub> y<sub>c</sub>)

answer: Example. For a 100 × 60 mm box with 2 mm walls, I<sub>xx</sub> = 2 × 200 × 30² + 2 × 2 × 60³/12 = 432,000 mm⁴; the dropped t³ term of the horizontal walls is 2 × 100 × 2³/12 = 133 mm⁴, 0.03 % of the total.

Applicability of bending theory. The simple theory is reliable for sizing, but three effects limit it: shear lag in wide skins raises the stress near the webs; local buckling and crippling of thin compressed walls lower their effective area; and plasticity near ultimate load redistributes stress.

Inclined wall example: a wall 60 mm long and 1 mm thick at 30° to x has t s³/12 = 18,000 mm⁴, so about its own centroid I<sub>xx,0</sub> = 18,000 sin²30° = 4,500 mm⁴, I<sub>yy,0</sub> = 13,500 mm⁴ and I<sub>xy,0</sub> = 7,794 mm⁴. Parallel-axis terms are added if its centroid is not at the section centroid.

Effective width in practice: for a compression skin between stringers only a strip near each stringer is counted with the stringer as the boom; the rest buckles and carries little extra load. This reduces I and raises the calculated stress, which is the safe direction.
Conclusion: the thin-walled theory is used for first sizing and stress estimates, then checked by effective-width rules, buckling checks, finite elements and tests.

bank.q: A section has I<sub>xx</sub> = 12 × 10⁶ mm⁴, I<sub>yy</sub> = 4 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and I<sub>xy</sub> = 2.5 × 10⁶ mm⁴. It carries M<sub>x</sub> = 8 kN·m and M<sub>y</sub> = 0. Find the direct stress at (40, 60) mm and the neutral-axis angle, and check the stress by the principal axis and neutral axis methods.

answer.text: Data in N and mm: I<sub>xx</sub> = 12 × 10⁶ mm⁴, I<sub>yy</sub> = 4 × 10⁶ mm⁴, I<sub>xy</sub> = 2.5 × 10⁶ mm⁴, M<sub>x</sub> = 8 × 10⁶ N·mm, M<sub>y</sub> = 0, point (40, 60) mm.
answer.pre: D = I<sub>xx</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − I<sub>xy</sub>² = 48 × 10¹² − 6.25 × 10¹² = 4.175 × 10¹³ mm⁸

answer.text: Constants:
answer.pre:
k₁ = (M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xx</sub> − M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D = −(8 × 10⁶ × 2.5 × 10⁶)/4.175 × 10¹³ = -0.4790 N/mm³
k₂ = (M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D = (8 × 10⁶ × 4 × 10⁶)/4.175 × 10¹³ = 0.7665 N/mm³

answer.text: Stress at the point:

answer: Neutral axis: tan α = −k₁/k₂ = I<sub>xy</sub>/I<sub>yy</sub> = 0.625, α = 32.0° from the x axis, towards +y.
Comparison: the simple formula M<sub>x</sub> y/I<sub>xx</sub> = 8 × 10⁶ × 60/12 × 10⁶ = 40.0 MPa overestimates this point by 13.2 MPa, because the point lies close to the tilted neutral axis.

answer.text: Check by the principal axis method:
answer.pre:
tan 2θ = −2 × 2.5/(12 − 4) = −0.625, θ = -16.00°
I<sub>u</sub>, I<sub>v</sub> = 8 × 10⁶ ± 4,716,991: I<sub>u</sub> = 12,716,991, I<sub>v</sub> = 3,283,009 mm⁴
M<sub>u</sub> = M<sub>x</sub> cos θ = 7,689,990 N·mm, M<sub>v</sub> = M<sub>x</sub> sin θ = -2,205,460 N·mm
u = 40 cos θ + 60 sin θ = 21.91 mm, v = 60 cos θ − 40 sin θ = 68.70 mm
σ = M<sub>u</sub> v/I<sub>u</sub> + M<sub>v</sub> u/I<sub>v</sub> = 41.54 + (-14.72) = 26.83 N/mm²

answer.text: Check by the neutral axis method:
answer.pre:
I<sub>NA</sub> = I<sub>xx</sub> cos²α + I<sub>yy</sub> sin²α − 2I<sub>xy</sub> sin α cos α = 7,505,618 mm⁴
M<sub>NA</sub> = M<sub>x</sub> cos α = 6,783,986 N·mm
n = y cos α − x sin α = 29.68 mm
σ = M<sub>NA</sub> n/I<sub>NA</sub> = 26.83 N/mm²

answer: Sign and meaning: the stress is tension because the point lies on the tension side of the neutral axis (above the line y = x tan 32.0°: at x = 40 the neutral axis is at y = 25.0 mm, and the point is at y = 60 mm).

Why the methods must agree: each is the same linear stress field σ = k₁ x + k₂ y written in different axes. The k method uses x, y directly; the neutral axis method uses the distance from the line σ = 0; the principal axis method uses u, v, where the two moment components act independently.
All three agree: σ = 26.83 MPa (tension) at (40, 60) mm, neutral axis at 32.0°.

bank.q: A Z-section has a 120 mm web and two 60 mm flanges, all 2.5 mm thick (top flange towards +x). It carries M<sub>x</sub> = 1.5 kN·m and M<sub>y</sub> = 0.4 kN·m. Find I<sub>xx</sub>, I<sub>yy</sub>, I<sub>xy</sub>, the neutral axis and the largest direct stress, and confirm by the principal axis method.
outline: Stress at web corners and flange tips
answer: Section: web 120 mm vertical, top flange 60 mm towards +x, bottom flange 60 mm towards −x, t = 2.5 mm. By antisymmetry the centroid is at the middle of the web.

answer.text: Section properties (thin-wall, t³ terms dropped):
Constants with M<sub>x</sub> = 1.5 × 10⁶ N·mm and M<sub>y</sub> = 0.4 × 10⁶ N·mm:

answer: Neutral axis: tan α = −k₁/k₂ = 0.7222, α = 35.8°.

answer.text: Stresses at the four extreme points:

answer: The largest stress is ±85.7 MPa at the web corners, the points farthest from the neutral axis.

answer.text: Check by the principal axis method:
Check by the neutral axis method at the top web corner:
answer.pre:
I<sub>NA</sub> = I<sub>xx</sub> cos²α + I<sub>yy</sub> sin²α − 2I<sub>xy</sub> sin α cos α = 557,160 mm⁴
M<sub>NA</sub> = M<sub>x</sub> cos α − M<sub>y</sub> sin α = 981,823 N·mm
n = 60 cos α = 48.64 mm,  σ = M<sub>NA</sub> n/I<sub>NA</sub> = 85.71 MPa

answer: Error of the symmetrical formula: M<sub>x</sub> y/I<sub>xx</sub> + M<sub>y</sub> x/I<sub>yy</sub> at the top web corner gives 1.5 × 10⁶ × 60/1,440,000 + 0 = 62.5 MPa, which is 23.2 MPa (27 %) too low; at the top flange tip it gives 62.5 + 0.4 × 10⁶ × 60/360,000 = 129.2 MPa against the true 23.8 MPa.

Interpretation: the neutral axis runs steeply through the web, so the web corners are the points farthest from it. A designer checks the web–flange junction, not the flange tips, for yield and for fatigue at rivets there.
Answer: I<sub>xx</sub> = 1,440,000, I<sub>yy</sub> = 360,000, I<sub>xy</sub> = 540,000 mm⁴; neutral axis 35.8°; σ<sub>max</sub> = ±85.7 MPa at the web corners.

bank.q: The 80 × 40 × 2 mm angle (I<sub>xx</sub> = 170,667 mm⁴, I<sub>yy</sub> = 32,000 mm⁴, I<sub>xy</sub> = −42,667 mm⁴) is an aluminium cantilever 800 mm long, E = 70 GPa, with a 50 N downward tip load through the centroid. Find the tip deflection and its direction, the root neutral axis and the root stresses.
outline: u and v at the tip
Root k₁, k₂, α and stresses
answer: Section properties (from the thin-wall angle example): I<sub>xx</sub> = 170,667 mm⁴, I<sub>yy</sub> = 32,000 mm⁴, I<sub>xy</sub> = −42,667 mm⁴, centroid 6.67 mm from the vertical leg and 26.67 mm above the horizontal leg.

answer.text: Moments for a cantilever of length L with a downward tip load W through the centroid: M<sub>x</sub> = W(L − z), positive (tension at the top), M<sub>y</sub> = 0. Curvatures:
answer.pre: u″ = M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>/(E D),   v″ = −M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>yy</sub>/(E D)

answer.text: Integrate twice with u = u′ = v = v′ = 0 at the root; ∫∫(L − z) dz dz = L³/3 at the tip:

answer: Resultant: √(-1.429² + -1.071²) = 1.786 mm, at -143.1° from +x: the tip moves down and towards −x.
Ignoring I<sub>xy</sub> would give v = −W L³/(3 E I<sub>xx</sub>) = -0.714 mm and no sideways movement: the true deflection is 2.5 times larger.
Root stresses: M<sub>x</sub> = 50 × 800 = 40,000 N·mm; k₁ = −M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>/D = 0.4687, k₂ = M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>yy</sub>/D = 0.3516 N/mm³; neutral axis at -53.1°.

answer.text: Stress at the extreme points (coordinates from the centroid):
Check by the principal axes:
answer.pre:
tan 2θ = −2I<sub>xy</sub>/(I<sub>xx</sub> − I<sub>yy</sub>), θ = 15.8°;  I<sub>u</sub> = 182,743, I<sub>v</sub> = 19,924 mm⁴
W<sub>u</sub> = −W sin θ = -13.62 N,  W<sub>v</sub> = −W cos θ = -48.11 N
δ<sub>u</sub> = W<sub>u</sub> L³/(3 E I<sub>v</sub>) = -1.666 mm,  δ<sub>v</sub> = W<sub>v</sub> L³/(3 E I<sub>u</sub>) = -0.642 mm
x = δ<sub>u</sub> cos θ − δ<sub>v</sub> sin θ = -1.429 mm,  y = δ<sub>u</sub> sin θ + δ<sub>v</sub> cos θ = -1.071 mm

answer: Why the tip moves mostly sideways: the load has a component along the weak principal axis (I<sub>v</sub> is only 19,924 mm⁴), and a small load along a very flexible direction gives a large movement.
Check: the deflection direction -143.1° differs from the neutral axis direction -53.1° by 90.0°, a right angle, as the theory requires.

bank.q: A wing box has booms at the corners of a 500 mm × 250 mm rectangle: front top 1000 mm², rear top 500 mm², rear bottom 500 mm², front bottom 800 mm². Outboard of the station the wing carries 5 kN/m lift and 1 kN/m drag over 3 m. Find the boom stresses.

answer.text: Moments at the station (x aft, y up). Lift 5 kN/m over the outboard 3 m compresses the top booms; drag 1 kN/m aft puts the front booms in tension:
Centroid of the booms (origin at boom 4, front bottom):
Section properties and boom stresses:
Constants:
answer.pre:
D = I<sub>xx</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − I<sub>xy</sub>² = 6.975 × 10¹⁵ mm⁸
k₁ = (M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xx</sub> − M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D = -0.04248 N/mm³
k₂ = (M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)/D = -0.52128 N/mm³

answer: Each boom stress in the table is σ = k₁ x + k₂ y.
Neutral axis: tan α = −k₁/k₂, α = -4.7°, nearly horizontal because the lift moment dominates.

Sign reasoning: x is aft and y up. Lift bends the wing up, so the lower booms stretch and the upper booms shorten: tension at negative y means M<sub>x</sub> < 0. Drag bends the wing aft, so the front booms (negative x) stretch: M<sub>y</sub> < 0.

Effect of I<sub>xy</sub>: ignoring it (σ = M<sub>x</sub> y/I<sub>xx</sub> + M<sub>y</sub> x/I<sub>yy</sub>) gives -55.0, -69.0, 60.2 and 74.2 MPa at booms 1 to 4. The worst compression would be underestimated by 5.2 MPa at boom 2.

What sets the moment: the lift moment grows with the square of the outboard length, so moving the station 1 m inboard (outboard length 4 m) would raise M<sub>x</sub> to −40 kN·m and every boom stress by the factor 40/22.5 = 1.78.
Answer: the most compressed boom is boom 2 (rear top, -74.2 MPa) and the most stretched boom 4 (front bottom, +77.4 MPa).

bank.q: An aluminium beam 50 mm wide and 120 mm deep spans 2 m, simply supported. Its top is at 60 °C and its bottom at 20 °C, varying linearly. Find the free curvature and mid-span bow, and the face stresses and restraining moment if the ends are clamped against rotation but free to extend.
answer: Data: aluminium, E = 70 GPa, α = 23 × 10⁻⁶ per K; section 50 mm wide, 120 mm deep; top at 60 °C, bottom at 20 °C, linear; span 2 m, simply supported.

answer.text: (a) Free curvature. The free strain is linear, so the beam bends without stress:
(b) Mid-span bow of the simply supported beam. A uniform curvature κ over a span L gives a circular arc with mid-span rise κ L²/8:
answer.pre: δ = 7.67 × 10⁻³ × 2.0²/8 = 0.00383 m = 3.83 mm, upwards (the hot top becomes convex)

answer: (c) Stress in the free beam: zero everywhere, because every fibre has exactly its free thermal strain.

answer.text: (d) Ends clamped against rotation, free to extend: curvature is prevented. The mean temperature is 40 °C, and σ = E α (T<sub>mean</sub> − T):
The restraining moment that holds the beam straight is the moment that would cause the free curvature:

answer: Check: M y/I = 3,864 × 0.060/7.20 × 10⁻⁶ = 32.2 MPa, equal to the face stress E α ΔT/2. The held-straight stress has zero net force but carries this moment, so it is not self-equilibrating.

Stress profile in the held-straight case: σ varies linearly with depth, from −32.2 MPa at the top through zero at mid-depth to +32.2 MPa at the bottom. Its net force is zero (equal and opposite triangles), so no axial restraint is needed, but its moment is not zero.

Physical check: the hot top wants to be longer than the cool bottom. Held straight, the top is shortened relative to its free length (compression) and the bottom lengthened (tension), as the signs show.
(e) If the ends were also prevented from extending, σ = −E α T, from −96.6 MPa at the top to −32.2 MPa at the bottom (temperatures measured as rises from a 0 °C stress-free state).

bank.q: Compare the neutral axis method, the k method and the principal axis method for unsymmetrical bending. Show on one numerical case that they agree, and say when each is most convenient.
outline: Neutral axis method formulas and use
Principal axis method formulas and use
answer: All three methods describe the same linear stress field σ = k₁ x + k₂ y, which is fixed by plane sections and the two moment conditions. They differ only in the order of the work.

answer.text: k method: compute D = I<sub>xx</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − I<sub>xy</sub>² and the constants, then evaluate at each point.
answer.pre: σ = (k<sub>a</sub> M<sub>x</sub> − k<sub>c</sub> M<sub>y</sub>) y + (k<sub>b</sub> M<sub>y</sub> − k<sub>c</sub> M<sub>x</sub>) x,  k<sub>a</sub> = I<sub>yy</sub>/D, k<sub>b</sub> = I<sub>xx</sub>/D, k<sub>c</sub> = I<sub>xy</sub>/D

answer: Best when one section carries many load cases: the three constants are found once.

answer.text: Neutral axis method: find α, then I<sub>NA</sub> and M<sub>NA</sub>, and take σ proportional to the distance from the neutral axis.
answer.pre:
tan α = (M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub> − M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xx</sub>)/(M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>yy</sub> − M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xy</sub>)
I<sub>NA</sub> = I<sub>xx</sub> cos²α + I<sub>yy</sub> sin²α − 2I<sub>xy</sub> sin α cos α,  M<sub>NA</sub> = M<sub>x</sub> cos α − M<sub>y</sub> sin α
σ = M<sub>NA</sub> n/I<sub>NA</sub>,  n = y cos α − x sin α

answer: Best when the question asks for the neutral axis and the largest stress: the farthest point from the neutral axis is found by eye.

answer.text: Principal axis method: find θ and I<sub>u</sub>, I<sub>v</sub>, resolve the moments and add two simple stresses.
answer.pre:
tan 2θ = −2I<sub>xy</sub>/(I<sub>xx</sub> − I<sub>yy</sub>);  M<sub>u</sub> = M<sub>x</sub> cos θ − M<sub>y</sub> sin θ,  M<sub>v</sub> = M<sub>x</sub> sin θ + M<sub>y</sub> cos θ
σ = M<sub>u</sub> v/I<sub>u</sub> + M<sub>v</sub> u/I<sub>v</sub>

answer: Best when the principal properties are tabulated (rolled angles) or the deflection is also wanted, since the deflection splits into two independent beams.

answer.text: Numerical equivalence on one case: I<sub>xx</sub> = 12 × 10⁶, I<sub>yy</sub> = 4 × 10⁶, I<sub>xy</sub> = 2.5 × 10⁶ mm⁴, M<sub>x</sub> = 8 kN·m, M<sub>y</sub> = 0, point (40, 60) mm.

answer: Errors to avoid: a wrong sign of I<sub>xy</sub> (tilts the axis the wrong way), the wrong pairing of M<sub>v</sub> with u, and coordinates measured from a corner instead of the centroid.

Where each fails in practice: the k method gives no picture of the neutral axis; the neutral axis method needs α to good accuracy because n is sensitive to it; the principal axis method needs care with the rotation signs. Using two methods catches all three kinds of slip.
Conclusion: choose the method that matches what is asked; the answer must not depend on it, so a second method is a good check.

bank.q: Show that a beam in unsymmetrical bending deflects perpendicular to its neutral axis, and discuss the consequences for Z-section stringers and wings.

answer.text: Curvatures. With u, v the deflections in x and y, a fibre at (x, y) has strain ε = −x u″ − y v″. Substituting σ = E ε into the moment conditions and solving gives:
answer.pre:
u″ = (M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>xy</sub> − M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xx</sub>)/(E D) = −k₁/E
v″ = (M<sub>y</sub> I<sub>xy</sub> − M<sub>x</sub> I<sub>yy</sub>)/(E D) = −k₂/E

answer: Direction. The curvature vector (u″, v″) is along (−k₁, −k₂). The neutral axis k₁ x + k₂ y = 0 has direction (k₂, −k₁). Their dot product is −k₁k₂ + k₂k₁ = 0, so the curvature, and hence the deflection, is perpendicular to the neutral axis at every station.

Symmetrical case. With I<sub>xy</sub> = 0 and M<sub>y</sub> = 0, k₁ = 0, the neutral axis is the x axis and the beam deflects along y, in the plane of the load. Only then does the beam move in the direction of the load.

answer.text: Z-section demonstration (I<sub>xx</sub> = 666,667, I<sub>yy</sub> = 166,667, I<sub>xy</sub> = 250,000 mm⁴, cantilever 1.2 m, E = 70 GPa, W = 500 N down):
answer.pre:
u = W L³ I<sub>xy</sub>/(3 E D) = +21.16 mm,  v = −W L³ I<sub>yy</sub>/(3 E D) = −14.11 mm
resultant 25.43 mm at −33.7°;  neutral axis at +56.3°;  56.3° − (−33.7°) = 90.0°

answer: The tip moves more sideways than down. Ignoring I<sub>xy</sub> gives 6.17 mm straight down: wrong in size and direction.
Consequences for stringers: a Z or angle stringer on its own would push sideways on the skin and twist the panel; it is riveted to the skin and held by clips so that it bends about the skin plane.

Consequences for wings: the bending direction of a box with unequal caps or composite skins is not the lift direction; with sweep this changes the local angle of attack and feeds aeroelastic calculations.

answer.text: Second demonstration, the 80 × 40 × 2 angle as an 800 mm cantilever with a 50 N downward tip load:
answer.pre:
u = -1.429 mm, v = -1.071 mm, direction -143.1°
neutral axis at the root: -53.1°;  difference 90.0°

answer: Principal-axes view: on u and v the two bending directions are independent. The load splits into components, each deflects in proportion to its own flexibility 1/I, and the resultant leans towards the axis with the smaller I. Only when the load lies along a principal axis, or I<sub>u</sub> = I<sub>v</sub>, does the beam move along the load.
Conclusion: deflection follows the neutral axis, not the load; the two agree only for bending about a principal axis.

bank.q: Discuss the validity of simple bending theory for thin-walled aircraft sections and state the corrections used in practice.
answer: Assumptions of the simple theory: plane sections; uniform direct stress across each thin wall; linear elastic material; small deflections; the shape of the section is kept (no distortion).
What holds well for aircraft sections: the thin-wall approximation itself (t/s small) and the boom idealisation; the general formula with I<sub>xy</sub> handles any shape, open or closed.

Limitation 1, shear lag: in a wide skin between webs the direct stress is not uniform; it peaks near the webs and falls between them. Correction: an effective width of skin, or a finite element model, and design for the peak stress.

Limitation 2, local buckling and crippling: thin compressed skin buckles below yield and then carries less load, shedding it to stringers. Correction: effective sheet width and crippling stress checks (see the chapters on stiffened panels and crippling).

Limitation 3, open sections under transverse load: unless the load passes through the shear centre, the section twists as well as bends. Correction: load through the shear centre or add the torsion analysis of the shear flow chapters.
Limitation 4, plasticity: near ultimate load the outer fibres yield and the stress redistributes. Correction: plastic or tangent-modulus methods for ultimate strength.
Limitation 5, temperature: gradients add stresses that the bending formula does not show. Correction: the thermal force and moment terms of the temperature chapter.
Limitation 6, large deflections and cut-outs: very flexible wings and panels with holes break the small-deflection and plane-section assumptions locally.

Evaluation with numbers: in the stringer box example, ignoring I<sub>xy</sub> changed the worst boom stress from −151.3 to −137.5 MPa, a 9 % unsafe error; in the Z-section, using M y/I gave 75.0 MPa against 171.4 MPa. Getting the general formula right matters more than these corrections in many exam problems, but in design each correction can be 10 % or more.

Shear lag in more detail: the skin receives its direct stress through shear from the spar webs. Far from the webs the skin strains less, so near a wide cut-out or at the root of a wide box the stress near the webs can be well above M y/I.

Crippling in more detail: a stringer's thin flanges buckle locally and the corners carry on until they yield; the average stress at failure, the crippling stress, can be well below the material's compressive yield for thin sections.

Conclusion: thin-walled bending theory is the right tool for sizing and first stress estimates; final design uses effective widths, buckling and crippling checks, shear-centre loading, thermal terms and finite element or test confirmation.

bank.q: A free beam has four 400 mm² booms at (±250, ±100) mm and carries M<sub>x</sub> = −20 kN·m. Boom 1 at (250, 100), next to a hot duct, is 60 K warmer than the others (E = 70 GPa, α = 23 × 10⁻⁶ per K). Find the total boom stresses and say when the thermal part can be ignored.
answer: Data: four booms of 400 mm² at (±250, ±100) mm, E = 70 GPa, α = 23 × 10⁻⁶ per K; M<sub>x</sub> = −20 kN·m (lift); boom 1 at (250, 100) is 60 K warmer than the rest. The beam is free.

answer.text: Section: symmetric, I<sub>xy</sub> = 0.
Bending stresses: σ<sub>b</sub> = M<sub>x</sub> y/I<sub>xx</sub>:
answer.pre:
top booms (y = +100): −2.0 × 10⁷ × 100/1.6 × 10⁷ = −125.0 MPa
bottom booms: +125.0 MPa

answer.text: Thermal stresses. With s = E α T₁ = 70,000 × 23 × 10⁻⁶ × 60 = 96.6 N/mm², the thermal force and moments are N<sub>T</sub> = sA, M<sub>xT</sub> = sA × 100, M<sub>yT</sub> = sA × 250. Then:
Superpose (the material is elastic):

answer: Checks: the thermal column sums to zero and has zero moments about both axes (self-equilibrating); the totals still give ΣAσ = 0 and ΣAσy = 400 × 100 × (−149.15 − 100.85) + 400 × (−100) × (100.85 + 149.15) = −2.0 × 10⁷ N·mm = M<sub>x</sub>.
Result: heating boom 1 raises its compression from 125.0 to 149.15 MPa (+19 %), and also loads boom 4 to +149.15 MPa. A design that ignored the duct would be unsafe at boom 1.

Physical reading: the hot boom pushes the beam into an extra bend and stretch. Booms 2 and 4 are pulled along although they are cold, so they gain tension; boom 3 is shortened and gains compression; boom 1 cannot expand as much as it wants and gains compression.

When the thermal part can be ignored: if the temperature field is linear in x and y and the beam is free, the thermal stress is zero. It cannot be ignored when the field is local (one hot boom) or the supports restrain the thermal bending.
